raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old male was referred for blurred disk margins and possible papilledema from his optometrist. He was visually asymptomatic. He had been seen in a hematology-oncology clinic one month prior for swollen groin lymph nodes that were noted to be reactive, but of unknown etiology. He had not had any previous STDs, genital lesions, penile discharge, or rash.
On exam, visual acuity was 20/25+ OD and 20/20- OS. Ishihara color plates were 11/11 OU. He had a trace afferent pupillary defect OS. Intraocular pressures were 12 OD and 18 OS. He had asymmetric disc edema, greater in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography showed a retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) average thickness of 188 microns OS with concentric circumferential elevation and an average RNFL thickness of 118 OD with inferonasal elevation (Figure 1).
Brain MRI and MRV with and without contrast were unremarkable, without mass lesions or venous occlusion. He underwent a lumbar puncture which showed a normal opening pressure of 18 cm H2O, normal protein, and glucose, and 72 white cells/mm3, predominately lymphocytes. Within 2 weeks of presentation, he developed headaches and eye pain, especially when bending over. Repeat examination showed worsening disc edema in the right eye and enlargement of the blind spot on visual field testing. Because his presentation was not consistent with papilledema, orbit MRI was performed, which showed increased optic nerve sheath fluid, especially posterior to the globes (Figure 2) and contrast enhancement of the optic nerve sheaths. Since the clinical and imaging findings appeared consistent with optic perineuritis, he was tested for secondary causes. He tested positive for syphilis with a rapid plasma reagent (RPR), with a titer of 1 : 128. FTA-ABS measured for confirmation was also positive. HIV testing was negative. He was placed on IV Penicillin 3,000,000 Units every 4 hours for 14 days. Repeat testing two weeks after antibiotic treatment showed marked improvement in both his symptoms and the extent of disc edema (Figure 3). Visual field testing also improved after antibiotics, with resolution of the enlarged blind spot (Figure 4).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old visually asymptomatic male was referred by his optometrist for bilateral blurred optic disc margins, subsequently developing headaches and pain on eye movement/bending over within 2 weeks.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Initially visually asymptomatic when referred for suspected papilledema, the patient developed headaches and ocular pain exacerbated by bending over within 2 weeks of presentation, accompanied by worsening right optic disc edema and blind spot enlargement.
subjective.past_medical_history: Evaluated in a hematology-oncology clinic 1 month prior for reactive inguinal lymphadenopathy of unknown etiology. Denied any history of prior STDs, genital lesions, urethral discharge, or skin rash.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initially asymptomatic; developed headache and ocular pain on bending forward 2 weeks after presentation. Denied prior genital ulcers or rash.

objective.physical_examination: Initial visual acuity was 20/25+ OD and 20/20- OS, with intact color vision (Ishihara 11/11 OU), a trace relative afferent pupillary defect OS, and intraocular pressures of 12 mmHg OD and 18 mmHg OS. Fundoscopy revealed asymmetric bilateral optic disc edema (initially greater in OS, with worsening OD edema at 2 weeks).
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline OCT showed circumferential RNFL thickening averaging 188 um OS and inferonasal RNFL elevation averaging 118 um OD; automated perimetry at 2 weeks showed blind spot enlargement. Brain MRI and MR venography (MRV) were normal without mass or venous sinus thrombosis, whereas dedicated contrast-enhanced orbital MRI demonstrated increased retrobulbar optic nerve sheath fluid and avid gadolinium enhancement of the optic nerve sheaths diagnostic of bilateral optic perineuritis. Lumbar puncture revealed a normal opening pressure of 18 cmH2O, normal protein and glucose, and lymphocytic pleocytosis of 72 WBCs/mm3.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed bilateral syphilitic optic perineuritis with neurosyphilis, established via high-titer serum RPR (1:128), positive serum FTA-ABS, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis (72 WBC/mm3), and perineural optic nerve sheath enhancement on orbital MRI. Treated with intravenous aqueous penicillin G 3,000,000 units every 4 hours for 14 days, resulting in marked resolution of headaches, optic disc edema, and visual field blind spot enlargement at 2 weeks post-treatment.
